```{r}
dir.create(figures_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

}

sim_rds <- paste0(
  "module1_simulation_1998_2040_",
  simulation_version,
  "_nsim_",

write_result_csv <- function(data, file_name) {
  readr::write_csv(data, file.path(tables_dir, file_name), na = "")
  invisible(data)
}

save_result_rds <- function(object, file_name) {
  saveRDS(object, file.path(results_dir, file_name))
  invisible(object)
}

weighted_sd <- function(x, w) {
  keep <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(w) & w > 0
  x <- x[keep]
  w <- w[keep]

  if (length(x) < 2L || sum(w) <= 0) return(NA_real_)

  mu <- weighted.mean(x, w)
  sqrt(sum(w * (x - mu)^2) / sum(w))
}

bmi_cat <- function(bmi) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    is.na(bmi)   ~ NA_character_,
    bmi < 18.5   ~ "underweight",
    bmi < 25.0   ~ "normal_weight",
    bmi < 30.0   ~ "overweight",
    bmi < 35.0   ~ "obesity_I",
    bmi < 40.0   ~ "obesity_II",
    TRUE         ~ "obesity_III"
  )
}
```

## Model Overview

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Model at a glance**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Model name / software** | PONTE-PT |
| **Setting** | Portugal (national, adult population) |
| **Perspective** | Population epidemiology and NHS cost perspective |
| **Simulated population** | Adults aged 20–84, initialised from NHS 1998 |
| **Horizon** | 1998–2040 (43 years) |
| **Cycle length** | 1 year |
| **Key outputs** | BMI/obesity trajectories, QALYs, healthcare cost scenario |
| **Price year** | 2018 euros (cost baseline); 2026 present value also shown |
| **Development status** | Single stochastic run; no Monte Carlo uncertainty quantified |
:::

> **Interpretation of current results.** All numerical results are based on one stochastic simulation run. Monte Carlo uncertainty has not yet been quantified; estimates should therefore be interpreted as illustrative of current model behaviour rather than stable point estimates. Stochastic uncertainty analysis using repeated simulations is planned before final reporting.

* * *

The Portuguese implementation is provided through **PONTE-PT**, an open-source, modular R package for annual dynamic microsimulation. It models adult BMI trajectories, mortality, health-related quality of life, and obesity-attributable economic outcomes.

The package separates general model logic from Portuguese parameter inputs. It can therefore be adapted to other jurisdictions after local data replacement, calibration, and validation.

@fig-model-overview summarises the annual simulation cycle, Portugal-specific inputs, outcome modules, and internal diagnostics.

### R Package Implementation

PONTE-PT is loaded from the local development repository using `devtools::load_all()`. Its core functions prepare model inputs; construct synthetic BMI cohorts; estimate annual BMI transitions; initialise and update the simulated population; apply mortality; add entrant cohorts; calculate QALYs; estimate obesity-attributable costs; and generate validation diagnostics.

Reproducibility is supported by version-controlled source code, fixed random seeds, structured input objects, automated output exports, and this Quarto-based reporting workflow. This report applies the Portuguese parameter set. The simulation logic is reusable, but transferring the model to another setting requires reassessment of population, BMI-transition, demographic, mortality, utility, and cost inputs.

The analysis was run using the development version of PONTE-PT (version `r packageVersion("pontept")`), rendered on `r Sys.Date()`.


### Jurisdictional Transferability

The table below distinguishes components that are generally reusable from those requiring replacement or reassessment when adapting PONTE-PT to another jurisdiction.

| Parameter group | Portuguese implementation | Requirement for another jurisdiction |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline population | NHS-based synthetic 1998 adult population | Replace with a local representative baseline population |
| BMI dynamics | Synthetic cohorts from Portuguese NHS waves | Re-estimate using local repeated cross-sectional or longitudinal data |
| Entrant cohorts | NHS donor pools and survey-weight targets | Replace with local entrant distributions and population targets |
| Mortality and demography | Portuguese life table and demographic inputs | Replace with local mortality and demographic data |
| Relative risks | Literature-derived BMI and education mortality RRs | Assess local applicability; use local estimates where possible |
| Utilities | Portuguese EQ-5D-5L age norms and external BMI decrements | Replace or reassess local valuation and utility evidence |
| Costs | Portuguese NHS 2018 direct-cost matrix | Replace with local payer-perspective costs and price year |
| Model logic | Annual individual updating and outcome aggregation | Reusable subject to structural-assumption review |
| Validation routines | Automated comparison framework | Reuse with local targets and predefined criteria |

* * *

## Verification, Validation, and Uncertainty

This section describes the current model-assurance status of the PONTE-PT
Portuguese implementation, following the ISPOR–SMDM Reports 1-7 (https://www.ispor.org/heor-resources/good-practices/article/modeling-good-research-practices---overview)

### Technical Verification

PONTE-PT includes automated unit tests for selected core functions, including BMI categorisation, mortality application, population ageing, entrant generation, synthetic-cohort construction, BMI-transition estimation, annual state advancement, QALY calculation, cost attribution, and input validation. Fixed random seeds support reproducible simulation runs. Input validators check required fields, age ranges, BMI values, positive survey weights, life-table structure, and donor-pool requirements.

During development, tests identified issues in the population-ageing cap, synthetic-cohort transition test fixtures following a schema change from same-age to cohort-forward matching, and QALY output-column naming. These issues were resolved. The current test suite contains **321 automated unit tests, all passing**.

**Planned verification activities** include deterministic-value tests, boundary and extreme-value tests, individual-level trace analyses, population-accounting checks, and comparison of selected outputs with hand calculations or analytically expected values.


### **Face Validity: Co-author Review Requested**
Co-authors are invited to review as expert the model’s face validity as part of their review of this technical report.

Please assess, within your area of expertise:

1. Whether the conceptual pathways adequately represent the relationships intended to be modelled.

  
2. Whether the temporal ordering of demographic, BMI, disease, mortality, and economic processes is logical and internally consistent.

3. Whether parameter choices, data sources, and modelling assumptions are appropriate and sufficiently justified.

4. Whether key assumptions are transparent, plausible, and relevant to the intended Portuguese policy applications.

5. Whether the direction and patterns of selected outputs appear plausible, including BMI trajectories, disease outcomes, costs, health outcomes, and socioeconomic inequalities.

Please identify:

1. Missing pathways, states, mechanisms, parameters, or policy-relevant outcomes.
2. Assumptions or parameter choices requiring clarification, revision, or stronger justification.
3. Implausible model behaviour or output patterns.
4. Recommended changes to the model, analysis, reporting, or documentation.


All comments will be recorded in a response log, together with the action taken and rationale. In subsequent reporting, this activity will be described as an internal expert face-validity review involving co-authors with expertise in dynamic microsimulation, health economics, obesity epidemiology, and social epidemiology. It will not be presented as independent external validation.

### Current Validation Status

The table below summarises the current assurance status of each model component, using the ISPOR–SMDM distinction between dependent targets used in model development and independent targets not used for that purpose.

The NHS 2005, 2014, and 2019 survey waves contributed to BMI-transition estimation and/or entrant-pool construction. Comparisons with these data are therefore dependent temporal calibration diagnostics rather than independent external validation. Across the six sex-by-year comparisons, simulated obesity prevalence was consistently lower than observed prevalence, with a mean absolute error of 3.37 percentage points.

| Component | Empirical target | Used in development? | Classification | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline BMI distribution | NHS 1998 | Yes | Initialisation integrity check | Agreement exact by construction; not predictive |
| Obesity prevalence 2005/2014/2019 | NHS waves | Yes | Dependent temporal calibration | Calibration plot, signed error, MAE 3.37 pp, RMSE 3.39 pp |
| Mortality rates | Portuguese life table | Yes | Internal consistency check | Age–sex rates vs. life-table input; single run |
| QALYs | No external target | — | Illustrative output | Population-weighted totals only; not externally validated |
| Costs | Borges et al. 2018 matrix | Yes | Input-based exploratory scenario | Published baseline rescaled by simulated prevalence |
| Independent BMI validation | No withheld source | — | Not yet implemented | Requires a withheld NHS wave or independent survey |



### Uncertainty

As noted above, the current report is based on one stochastic simulation run and does not quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty. Before final reporting, stochastic uncertainty will be assessed using at least 100 independent simulation replications with different random seeds and a pre-specified population size per replication.

## 1 Input Preparation

Model inputs were prepared before simulation and comprise the 1998 baseline population, repeated NHS BMI data, mortality life tables, entrant donor pools, and model settings. The analysis loads this prepared input object and validates its required components before simulation.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-inputs

prepared_inputs_file <- file.path(
  project_root,
  "data-raw",
  "model_inputs_prepared.rds"
)

prepare_script_file <- file.path(
  project_root,
  "data-raw",
  "prepare_model_inputs.R"
)

if (!file.exists(prepared_inputs_file)) {
  if (!file.exists(prepare_script_file)) {
    stop(
      "Neither prepared inputs nor preparation script were found:\n",
      prepared_inputs_file, "\n",
      prepare_script_file,
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }

  old_wd <- getwd()
  on.exit(setwd(old_wd), add = TRUE)
  setwd(project_root)

  source(prepare_script_file, local = new.env(parent = globalenv()))

  if (!file.exists(prepared_inputs_file)) {
    stop(
      "`prepare_model_inputs.R` completed but did not create:\n",
      prepared_inputs_file,
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
}

inputs <- readRDS(prepared_inputs_file)

required_input_names <- c(
  "population_1998",
  "bmi_panel",
  "life_table",
  "donor_pool_1998",
  "donor_pool_2005",
  "donor_pool_2014",
  "donor_pool_2019",
  "settings"
)

missing_inputs <- setdiff(required_input_names, names(inputs))

if (length(missing_inputs) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "Model inputs missing: ",
    paste(missing_inputs, collapse = ", "),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

population_1998 <- inputs$population_1998
bmi_panel <- inputs$bmi_panel
life_table <- inputs$life_table
donor_pool_1998 <- inputs$donor_pool_1998
donor_pool_2005 <- inputs$donor_pool_2005
donor_pool_2014 <- inputs$donor_pool_2014
donor_pool_2019 <- inputs$donor_pool_2019
settings_base <- inputs$settings
```

```{r}
#| label: validate-donor-pools
#| include: false

donor_pools <- list(
  `1998` = donor_pool_1998,
  `2005` = donor_pool_2005,
  `2014` = donor_pool_2014,
  `2019` = donor_pool_2019
)

purrr::walk(
  donor_pools,
  \(pool) ponte_validate_entrant_donor_pool(donor_pool = pool)
)

donor_pool_sizes <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  donor_pools,
  \(pool, wave_year) tibble::tibble(
    wave_year = as.integer(wave_year),
    donor_records = nrow(pool),
    weighted_population = sum(pool$survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)

write_result_csv(donor_pool_sizes, "module1_donor_pool_sizes.csv")
```

## 2 Derived Inputs

Three objects must be constructed before the simulation can run:

- **`rr_bmi`** — all-cause mortality relative risks by BMI category and sex,
  with normal weight as reference. Relative risks are based on the Global BMI
  Mortality Collaboration meta-analysis [@DiAngelantonio2016].

- **`rr_education`** — all-cause mortality relative risks by education level,
  based on the IHME-CHAIN Collaborators meta-analysis [@IHMECHAIN2024].

- **`bmi_transition_model`** — synthetic-cohort BMI-transition model fitted
  from repeated Portuguese NHS cross-sections.

```{r}
#| label: build-rr-bmi

rr_bmi <- tibble::tribble(
  ~sex,      ~bmi_category,    ~rr_bmi,
  "men",     "underweight",    1.85,
  "men",     "normal_weight",  1.00,
  "men",     "overweight",     0.94,
  "men",     "obesity_I",      1.12,
  "men",     "obesity_II",     1.42,
  "men",     "obesity_III",    1.92,
  "women",   "underweight",    1.82,
  "women",   "normal_weight",  1.00,
  "women",   "overweight",     0.97,
  "women",   "obesity_I",      1.09,
  "women",   "obesity_II",     1.38,
  "women",   "obesity_III",    1.85
)
```

```{r}
#| label: build-rr-education

# Mackenbach et al. (2024), Lancet Public Health.
# Lower education carries higher all-cause mortality risk.
rr_education <- tibble::tibble(
  education_level2 = c("lower", "higher"),
  rr_education = c(1.20, 0.90)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: build-bmi-model

bmi_panel_prepared <- ponte_prepare_bmi_panel(bmi_panel)

bmi_transitions <- ponte_build_bmi_synthetic_cohorts(
  bmi_panel_prepared
)

bmi_transition_model <- ponte_fit_bmi_transition(
  bmi_transitions,
  projection_period = 2014L
)
```

```{r}
#| label: validate-derived-inputs
#| include: false

ponte_validate_life_table(life_table)
ponte_validate_mortality_risks(
  rr_bmi = rr_bmi,
  rr_education = rr_education
)
```

## BMI-Transition Model

### Synthetic-cohort construction

Repeated Portuguese NHS cross-sectional survey waves from 1998, 2005, 2014,
and 2019 were used to construct synthetic cohorts. Because the NHS waves do not
follow the same respondents longitudinally, the synthetic cohorts represent
population groups with shared stable characteristics rather than observed
individual-level trajectories. BMI change is therefore inferred at the
synthetic-cohort level, not from individual follow-up data.

Synthetic cohorts were defined by **sex** (men, women), **education level**
(higher, lower), and **five-year age group at the baseline survey wave**
(12 groups: 20–24, 25–29, ..., 75–79 years). This gives 2 × 2 × 12 = 48
cohorts per transition interval.

Three consecutive survey-wave pairs were used, producing 144 synthetic
transitions in total:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-transition-intervals
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Synthetic-cohort transition intervals used to estimate annual BMI change. Each interval contributes 48 cohorts (2 sex × 2 education × 12 five-year age groups)."

bmi_transitions |>
  dplyr::distinct(year_t, year_t1) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    interval_years = year_t1 - year_t,
    n_cohorts      = 48L
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year_t) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Earlier NHS wave", "Later NHS wave",
                  "Interval (years)", "Cohorts")
  )
```

For each cohort observed in consecutive survey waves, weighted mean BMI was
calculated at the earlier ($t_0$) and later ($t_1$) wave using NHS survey
weights. The annual BMI change for cohort $c$ is:

$$
\Delta\mathrm{BMI}_{\mathrm{annual},\,c}
= \frac{\overline{\mathrm{BMI}}_{c,\,t_1} - \overline{\mathrm{BMI}}_{c,\,t_0}}{t_1 - t_0}
$$

The annualisation is exact: the maximum absolute difference between the stored
`annual_bmi_change` and the recomputed formula is zero (verified
programmatically). A transition weight equal to the geometric mean of the two
wave-level survey weights is assigned to each cohort.

### BMI updating in the simulation

In each annual simulation cycle, survivors’ BMI is updated by adding the predicted annual BMI change from the fitted transition model. BMI is retained as a continuous variable and recategorised after each update for obesity-prevalence, mortality-risk, utility, and cost calculations. Values are constrained to a plausible range of 10–80 kg/m² after each cycle. [https://github.com/NCD-RisC/Data-cleaning-protocol/blob/main/README.md]

The base case assumes that annual BMI-transition parameters remain constant after the final observed NHS wave in 2019. This stationarity assumption is structural and will be examined in scenario analyses. 



### BMI measurement

BMI in the Portuguese NHS is derived from self-reported height and weight. The base-case analysis does not correct for potential self-report bias.

**Planned sensitivity analysis.** BMI calibration equations will be applied to assess the effect of correcting self-reported height and weight.


### NHS wave characteristics

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bmi-transition-waves
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Portuguese NHS waves used for synthetic-cohort BMI-transition estimation, restricted to respondents aged 20–79 with valid BMI and survey weight."

bmi_panel |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% c(1998L, 2005L, 2014L, 2019L)) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    survey_records      = dplyr::n(),
    weighted_population = round(sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE)),
    mean_bmi            = round(weighted.mean(bmi, w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("NHS wave", "Survey records",
                  "Weighted population", "Weighted mean BMI (kg/m²)")
  )
```

### Education classification: three-level reporting versus binary transition model

The simulation population retains a three-level education variable for output
reporting: `low`, `medium`, and `high`. The BMI-transition model requires a
binary grouping: `education_level2`. The mapping is:

- **`low` and `medium`** → `lower` (used in BMI-transition estimation)
- **`high`** → `higher` (used in BMI-transition estimation)

Consequently, individuals with `low` and `medium` education receive identical
BMI-transition predictions; only the `high`-versus-`low`/`medium` contrast
is captured by the transition model. Separate transition estimates for `low`
and `medium` education would require sufficient sample sizes in the NHS waves
to sustain the additional grouping.

### BMI-transition handling for ages 80–84

Synthetic cohorts are defined only up to ages 75–79, whereas the simulation includes adults aged 80–84. The weighted ordinary least-squares transition model includes a quadratic age term:

$$\Delta\mathrm{BMI} \sim \mathrm{sex} + \mathrm{age} + \mathrm{age}^2 + \mathrm{education} + \mathrm{period}$$

For ages 80–84, predicted BMI change is extrapolated from this fitted age function beyond the observed age range. These predictions should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

### Annual event sequence

The following sequence is applied in each simulation year (transitioning the
state from year $t$ to year $t+1$):

1. **Mortality** — death probability assigned from life-table hazard × BMI and
   education RRs; deaths drawn stochastically and recorded with year $= t+1$.
2. **BMI updating** — survivors' BMI updated by the transition-model predicted
   annual change; BMI constrained to 10–80 kg/m².
3. **Demographic updating** — survivors aged by one year (capped at 84);
   calendar year advanced to $t+1$.
4. **Entrant generation** — age-20 entrants sampled from the period-appropriate
   donor pool, assigned year $= t+1$; survivors and entrants combined.

The simulation stores annual demographic and health states for each individual. Costs and QALYs are calculated subsequently by applying the relevant cost and utility inputs to these records.

### Key assumptions

- Repeated NHS cross-sections support synthetic-cohort estimates of population-level BMI change; they do not observe individual BMI trajectories.
- Synthetic cohorts are defined by sex, binary education level, and five-year baseline age group; these characteristics are treated as stable across survey waves.
- The base case assumes that annual BMI-transition parameters remain constant after 2019.
- BMI transitions for ages 80–84 are extrapolated beyond the observed 20–79-year age range.
- Uncertainty in BMI-transition parameter estimates is not yet propagated.

* * *

## 3 Module 1: Obesity Trajectories 1998–2040

The simulation is initialised in 1998 using the full NHS baseline population aged 20–84 years. From 1999 onwards, new age-20 entrants are sampled from period-specific donor pools. Comparisons with NHS data from 2005, 2014, and 2019 are reported as dependent temporal calibration diagnostics because these waves contributed to transition estimation and entrant-pool construction.

### 3.1 Simulation Settings

```{r}
#| label: settings-module1

settings_historical <- ponte_settings(
  initial_year = 1998L,
  projection_end_year = 2040L,
  entry_age = 20L,
  max_age = 84L,
  n_simulations = n_simulations_main,
  entrant_n_per_year = 100L,
  seed = 20260817L
)
```

### 3.2 Entrant Targets

Entrants are assigned the weighted age-20 NHS population size from the survey wave nearest to their entry year. The model uses the 1998 wave for entry years 1999–2004, the 2005 wave for 2005–2013, the 2014 wave for 2014–2018, and the 2019 wave for 2019–2040.

```{r}
#| label: entrant-targets-module1

entrant_by_wave <- bmi_panel |>
  filter(age == 20L, year %in% c(1998L, 2005L, 2014L, 2019L)) |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(
    entrant_population = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(wave_year = year)

entry_years <- seq.int(
  settings_historical$initial_year + 1L,
  settings_historical$projection_end_year
)

entrant_targets_historical <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  entry_year = entry_years,
  sex = c("men", "women")
) |>
  mutate(
    wave_year = case_when(
      entry_year <= 2004L ~ 1998L,
      entry_year <= 2013L ~ 2005L,
      entry_year <= 2018L ~ 2014L,
      TRUE ~ 2019L
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(entrant_by_wave, by = c("wave_year", "sex")) |>
  select(entry_year, sex, entrant_population) |>
  mutate(
    entry_year = as.integer(entry_year),
    entrant_population = as.numeric(entrant_population)
  ) |>
  arrange(entry_year, sex)

if (anyNA(entrant_targets_historical$entrant_population)) {
  stop(
    "Entrant targets are missing. Check bmi_panel includes age == 20 in all NHS waves.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

ponte_validate_entrant_targets(
  entrant_targets = entrant_targets_historical,
  start_year = settings_historical$initial_year + 1L,
  end_year = settings_historical$projection_end_year
)

write_result_csv(entrant_targets_historical, "module1_entrant_targets.csv")
```

### 3.3 Simulation

Simulation outputs are stored as versioned RDS files in `analysis/results/`. Increment `simulation_version` whenever changes to model inputs, parameters, or simulation logic affect results.

```{r}
#| label: run-module1
#| cache: false

donor_pools_module1 <- list(
  list(from = 1999L, to = 2004L, pool = donor_pool_1998),
  list(from = 2005L, to = 2013L, pool = donor_pool_2005),
  list(from = 2014L, to = 2018L, pool = donor_pool_2014),
  list(from = 2019L, to = 2040L, pool = donor_pool_2019)
)

sim_path <- file.path(results_dir, sim_rds)

if (file.exists(sim_path)) {
  simulation_historical <- readRDS(sim_path)

  cached_simulations <- dplyr::n_distinct(simulation_historical$simulation)
  if (cached_simulations != n_simulations_main) {
    stop(
      "Cached simulation has ", cached_simulations,
      " simulation(s), but n_simulations_main is ", n_simulations_main,
      ". Delete the stale cache or increment simulation_version.",
      call. = FALSE
    )
  }
} else {
  simulation_historical <- ponte_run_simulation(
    population = population_1998,
    settings = settings_historical,
    life_table = life_table,
    rr_bmi = rr_bmi,
    rr_education = rr_education,
    donor_pool = donor_pool_1998,
    donor_pools = donor_pools_module1,
    entrant_targets = entrant_targets_historical,
    bmi_transition_model = bmi_transition_model,
    bmi_update_method = "legacy",
    stochastic_bmi = TRUE,
    education_source = "existing",
    bmi_limits = c(10, 80)
  )

  save_result_rds(simulation_historical, sim_rds)
  write_result_csv(
    simulation_historical,
    paste0("module1_simulation_1998_2040_", simulation_version, ".csv")
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: summarise-module1
#| include: false

historical_living_summary <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(alive) |>
  mutate(obesity = bmi >= 30) |>
  group_by(year, sex, education_level, simulation) |>
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = weighted.mean(bmi, w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    obesity_prevalence = weighted.mean(obesity, w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    weighted_population = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_records = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(year, sex, education_level) |>
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(mean_bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    obesity_prevalence = mean(obesity_prevalence, na.rm = TRUE),
    weighted_population = mean(weighted_population, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_records = mean(n_records, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(year, sex, education_level)

write_result_csv(
  historical_living_summary,
  "module1_living_population_summary.csv"
)
```

### 3.4a Mortality Input Consistency Check

> **Classification:** Internal consistency check. The Portuguese life table is an input to the simulation; this comparison therefore assesses whether simulated mortality is consistent with the input structure rather than providing independent validation. Differences reflect BMI and education relative-risk adjustment and stochastic variation. Results should be reassessed across repeated simulation runs before drawing conclusions.

```{r}
#| label: mortality-consistency-check
#| include: false

age_breaks_mx <- c(20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 85)
age_labels_mx <- c("20–29", "30–39", "40–49", "50–59", "60–69", "70–79", "80–84")

lt_mx <- life_table |>
  mutate(
    mx_per1000 = -log1p(-qx) * 1000,
    age_band = cut(
      age,
      breaks = age_breaks_mx,
      right = FALSE,
      labels = age_labels_mx
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(age_band)) |>
  group_by(sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    lt_mx_per1000 = mean(mx_per1000, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sim_denom_1998 <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(year == 1998L, alive) |>
  mutate(
    age_band = cut(
      age,
      breaks = age_breaks_mx,
      right = FALSE,
      labels = age_labels_mx
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(age_band)) |>
  group_by(sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    population_weight = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sim_numer_1999 <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(year == 1999L, !alive) |>
  mutate(
    age_band = cut(
      age,
      breaks = age_breaks_mx,
      right = FALSE,
      labels = age_labels_mx
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(age_band)) |>
  group_by(sex, age_band) |>
  summarise(
    death_weight = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sim_mx_1998 <- sim_denom_1998 |>
  left_join(sim_numer_1999, by = c("sex", "age_band")) |>
  mutate(
    death_weight = replace_na(death_weight, 0),
    sim_mx_per1000 = 1000 * death_weight / population_weight
  )

mortality_consistency <- lt_mx |>
  left_join(sim_mx_1998, by = c("sex", "age_band")) |>
  mutate(
    mx_ratio = sim_mx_per1000 / lt_mx_per1000,
    mx_abs_diff = sim_mx_per1000 - lt_mx_per1000
  )

write_result_csv(
  mortality_consistency,
  "module1_mortality_consistency.csv"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mortality-consistency
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Mortality input consistency: life-table central death rate versus simulated death rate for the 1998 exposure period, by sex and age group. Deaths recorded in 1999 arise from the 1998 to 1999 transition. Differences reflect relative-risk adjustment and stochastic variation."

mortality_consistency |>
  mutate(
    lt_mx_per1000 = round(lt_mx_per1000, 2),
    sim_mx_per1000 = round(sim_mx_per1000, 2),
    mx_ratio = round(mx_ratio, 3),
    mx_abs_diff = round(mx_abs_diff, 2)
  ) |>
  select(sex, age_band, lt_mx_per1000, sim_mx_per1000, mx_ratio, mx_abs_diff) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Sex", "Age band", "Life-table mx / 1,000",
      "Simulated mx / 1,000", "Ratio (sim/LT)", "Difference (sim \u2212 LT), per 1,000"
    )
  )
```

### 3.5 Retrospective Calibration

Simulated obesity prevalence is compared with observed NHS prevalence in 2005, 2014, and 2019. These comparisons are dependent temporal calibration diagnostics because the corresponding NHS waves contributed to BMI-transition estimation and/or entrant-pool construction.

```{r}
#| label: module1-validation
#| include: false

validation_years <- c(2005L, 2014L, 2019L)

observed_prevalence <- bmi_panel |>
  filter(year %in% validation_years) |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(
    obesity_prevalence_observed = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    n_observed = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

simulated_prevalence <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(alive, year %in% validation_years) |>
  group_by(year, sex, simulation) |>
  summarise(
    obesity_prevalence = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(
    obesity_prevalence_simulated = mean(obesity_prevalence, na.rm = TRUE),
    sim_lo = if (report_uncertainty) {
      quantile(obesity_prevalence, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    sim_hi = if (report_uncertainty) {
      quantile(obesity_prevalence, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    n_simulations = n_distinct(simulation),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

validation_combined <- simulated_prevalence |>
  left_join(
    observed_prevalence |>
      select(year, sex, obesity_prevalence_observed, n_observed),
    by = c("year", "sex")
  ) |>
  arrange(year, sex)

validation_errors <- validation_combined |>
  mutate(
    signed_error = obesity_prevalence_simulated - obesity_prevalence_observed,
    absolute_error = abs(signed_error)
  )

mae <- mean(validation_errors$absolute_error, na.rm = TRUE)
rmse <- sqrt(mean(validation_errors$signed_error^2, na.rm = TRUE))

write_result_csv(
  validation_combined,
  "module1_validation_prevalence.csv"
)

write_result_csv(
  validation_errors,
  "module1_validation_errors.csv"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-module1-validation
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Dependent temporal calibration: simulated and observed NHS obesity prevalence at survey years. Interval estimates are shown only when at least 30 simulation runs are available."

if (report_uncertainty) {
  validation_combined |>
    mutate(
      obesity_prevalence_simulated = scales::percent(
        obesity_prevalence_simulated,
        accuracy = 0.1
      ),
      sim_lo = scales::percent(sim_lo, accuracy = 0.1),
      sim_hi = scales::percent(sim_hi, accuracy = 0.1),
      obesity_prevalence_observed = scales::percent(
        obesity_prevalence_observed,
        accuracy = 0.1
      )
    ) |>
    select(
      year, sex, obesity_prevalence_simulated,
      sim_lo, sim_hi, obesity_prevalence_observed
    ) |>
    knitr::kable(
      col.names = c(
        "Year", "Sex", "Simulated mean", "Sim. 2.5%",
        "Sim. 97.5%", "Observed (NHS)"
      )
    )
} else {
  validation_combined |>
    mutate(
      obesity_prevalence_simulated = scales::percent(
        obesity_prevalence_simulated,
        accuracy = 0.1
      ),
      obesity_prevalence_observed = scales::percent(
        obesity_prevalence_observed,
        accuracy = 0.1
      )
    ) |>
    select(year, sex, obesity_prevalence_simulated, obesity_prevalence_observed) |>
    knitr::kable(
      col.names = c("Year", "Sex", "Simulated", "Observed (NHS)")
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-module1-validation
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Dependent temporal calibration of obesity prevalence: simulated estimates versus observed NHS prevalence at 2005, 2014, and 2019. Circles denote simulated estimates and crosses denote observed NHS prevalence. Simulation intervals are displayed only for at least 30 runs."

validation_plot <- ggplot(
  validation_combined,
  aes(x = factor(year), colour = sex, group = sex)
) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = obesity_prevalence_simulated),
    size = 2.5,

    shape = 4,
    size = 3.5,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Survey year",
    y = "Obesity prevalence",
    colour = "Sex",
    caption = if (report_uncertainty) {
      "Circles = simulated mean; error bars = 95% simulation interval; crosses = observed NHS."
    } else {
      "Circles = one simulated run; crosses = observed NHS. Interval estimates require at least 30 runs."
    }
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

if (report_uncertainty) {
  validation_plot <- validation_plot +
    geom_errorbar(
      aes(ymin = sim_lo, ymax = sim_hi),
      width = 0.15,
      position = position_dodge(width = 0.3)
    )
}

validation_plot
```

### 3.6 Calibration Error Metrics

```{r}
#| label: module1-error-metrics
#| echo: false

calibration_metrics <- tibble::tibble(
  metric = c("Mean absolute error", "Root mean squared error"),
  value = c(mae, rmse)
)

calibration_metrics |>
  # Values are proportions; multiply by 100 to express as percentage points.
  # Do not use scales::percent() — the errors are differences in prevalence
  # (percentage points), not ratios.
  mutate(value = paste0(round(value * 100, 2), " pp")) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Metric", "Value (percentage points)"))
```

Across the six sex-by-year comparisons, simulated obesity prevalence was lower than observed prevalence in every case,  indicating systematic underestimation.

## 4 Module 2: Quality-adjusted Life Years

### 4.1 Population-weighted QALYs

QALYs are calculated for simulated individuals who are alive using age-specific Portuguese EQ-5D-5L utility norms [@Ferreira2023]. BMI-related utility decrements are applied to individuals with BMI ≥25 kg/m² using published estimates for overweight and obesity [@OverweightUtilityReview2021]. No decrement is applied to underweight BMI because the selected evidence covers overweight and obesity only.

The module reports annual population-weighted QALY totals for the living simulated population. These totals reflect both the number of people alive and their health-related quality of life. They are not per-person QALYs, estimates of education-related QALY inequality, or externally validated measures of disease burden.

The current implementation does not estimate GBD-comparable years of life lost, years lived with disability, or disability-adjusted life years. Estimating these outcomes would require a specified reference life table, cause-specific disability weights, and validation against appropriate Portuguese or GBD estimates.

```{r}
#| label: run-module2-qalys
#| cache: false

qaly_results <- ponte_calculate_qalys(
  simulation_output = simulation_historical,
  min_age = 20L,
  max_age = 84L
)

if (!"by_year" %in% names(qaly_results)) {
  stop(
    "`ponte_calculate_qalys()` must return an object named `by_year`.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}


write_result_csv(
  qaly_results$by_year,
  "module2_qalys_by_year.csv"
)

if ("overall" %in% names(qaly_results)) {
  write_result_csv(
    qaly_results$overall,
    "module2_qalys_overall.csv"
  )
}

qaly_results_total <- qaly_results$by_year |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    total_qalys_weighted = sum(mean_total_qalys_weighted, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-module2-qalys-overall
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Annual total population-weighted QALYs accrued by the living simulated population, 1998–2040."

qaly_results_total |>
  summarise(
    mean_annual_total_qalys = mean(total_qalys_weighted, na.rm = TRUE),
    cumulative_total_qalys  = sum(total_qalys_weighted,  na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 0))) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Mean annual total QALYs (weighted)",
      "Cumulative QALYs, 1998–2040 (weighted)"
    )
  )
```

## 5 Module 3: Exploratory High-BMI Attributable-Cost Scenario {#sec-module3}

This exploratory, simulation-linked scenario adapts the Portuguese 2018 overweight-and-obesity cost-of-illness framework reported by Borges et al. [@Borges2025]. It applies the published 2018 direct medical cost matrix to disease-specific high-BMI population-attributable fractions (PAFs) derived from simulated BMI-category prevalence and GBD 2019 relative-risk functions.

The analysis is not a direct reproduction of the Borges et al. estimate. It replaces the INSEF-based exposure prevalence used in the source study with simulated 2018 prevalence and approximates the continuous GBD BMI exposure distribution using two discrete categories. Results should therefore be interpreted as exploratory scenario estimates rather than externally validated estimates of Portuguese healthcare costs.

High BMI is represented by mutually exclusive overweight (BMI 25.0–29.9 kg/m²) and obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) categories. Within each age-sex stratum, PAFs combine simulated category-specific prevalence with relative risks evaluated at representative BMI values of 27.5 kg/m² for overweight and 32.5 kg/m² for obesity, each relative to BMI 22 kg/m².

Published direct treatment costs for overweight and obesity are included at 100% attribution because they are already assigned to the high-BMI exposure. Depression costs are retained for descriptive purposes but excluded from the attributable total because the current analysis does not apply a BMI-to-depression relative-risk function.

### 5.1 Source Study and Exposure Definition

Borges et al. estimated Portuguese direct medical costs attributable to overweight and obesity combined using INSEF 2015 prevalence estimates and a high-BMI definition of BMI ≥25 kg/m². The published prevalence estimates were:

- Overweight (BMI 25.0–29.9 kg/m²): 45.4% among men, 33.1% among women, and 38.9% overall.
- Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²): 24.9% among men, 32.1% among women, and 28.7% overall.
- High BMI (BMI ≥25 kg/m²): 70.3% among men and 65.2% among women.

The present analysis retains the published 2018 cost matrix but uses simulated 2018 BMI-category prevalence in the PAF calculations. @tbl-module3-exposure-prevalence compares the published INSEF 2015 prevalence estimates with the corresponding simulated values.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-module3-exposure-prevalence
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Published INSEF 2015 prevalence estimates reported by Borges et al. [@Borges2025] and simulated 2018 BMI-category prevalence used in the exploratory high-BMI cost scenario."

simulated_bmi_prevalence_2018 <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(alive, year == 2018L) |>
  dplyr::group_by(sex) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    p_overweight = weighted.mean(bmi >= 25 & bmi < 30, w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    p_obesity    = weighted.mean(bmi >= 30,             w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    p_high_bmi   = weighted.mean(bmi >= 25,             w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    sex    = dplyr::recode(sex, men = "Males", women = "Females"),
    source = "Simulated population, 2018"
  )

dplyr::bind_rows(
  obesity_prevalence_2018() |> dplyr::mutate(source = "INSEF 2015 / Borges et al."),
  simulated_bmi_prevalence_2018
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::ends_with("bmi") | dplyr::starts_with("p_"),
                              \(x) scales::percent(x, accuracy = 0.1))) |>
  dplyr::select(source, sex, p_overweight, p_obesity, p_high_bmi) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Source", "Sex", "Overweight", "Obesity", "BMI \u226525 kg/m\u00b2")
  )
```

### 5.2 Published 2018 Cost Inputs

```{r}
#| label: tbl-module3-published-cost-inputs
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Published Portuguese direct medical cost inputs for overweight and obesity in 2018, by disease group [@Borges2025]. Values are thousands of 2018 euros, ordered by total cost."

# Load cost data here so this table is self-contained, regardless of chunk
# execution order. The main load-cost-inputs chunk will reassign the same
# objects later without conflict.
costs_2018 <- obesity_direct_costs_2018()

disease_labels <- tibble::tribble(
  ~disease_group,               ~description,
  "obesity_overweight",         "Overweight and obesity treatment (direct)",
  "diabetes_mellitus_type_2",   "Type 2 diabetes mellitus",
  "ischaemic_heart_disease",    "Ischaemic heart disease",
  "stroke",                     "Stroke",
  "hypertensive_hd_af",         "Hypertensive heart disease and atrial fibrillation",
  "cancer_all",                 "Obesity-related cancers (all)",
  "osteoarthritis",             "Osteoarthritis",
  "gout",                       "Gout",
  "depression",                 "Depression (excluded from attributable total)",
  "alzheimers_disease",         "Alzheimer's disease",
  "chronic_kidney_disease",     "Chronic kidney disease",
  "gallbladder_biliary_diseases","Gallbladder and biliary diseases",
  "asthma",                     "Asthma",
  "cataracts",                  "Cataracts"
)

costs_2018 |>
  dplyr::left_join(disease_labels, by = "disease_group") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(total)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(inpatient, outpatient, pharmacological, total),
                              \(x) round(x, 0))) |>
  dplyr::select(description, inpatient, outpatient, pharmacological, total) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Disease group", "Inpatient (k\u20ac)",
                  "Outpatient (k\u20ac)", "Pharmacological (k\u20ac)", "Total (k\u20ac)")
  )
```

### 5.3 GBD Relative Risks for PAF Derivation

Disease-specific BMI relative-risk functions were obtained from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019 relative-risk dataset [@GBD2019RR]. In the GBD comparative risk-assessment framework, high BMI is represented as a continuous exposure, with age- and sex-specific relative-risk functions for selected disease outcomes.

In this scenario, those functions are evaluated at representative BMI values of 27.5 kg/m² for overweight and 32.5 kg/m² for obesity, each relative to BMI 22 kg/m². This two-category approach approximates, but does not reproduce, the continuous BMI exposure distribution used in the GBD framework.

```{r}
#| label: load-gbd-rr
#| include: false

gbd_rr_path <- file.path(
  project_root,
  "data-raw",
  "GBD_RR_2019",
  "gbd_rr_2019.xlsx"
)

if (!file.exists(gbd_rr_path)) {
  stop(
    "GBD relative-risk workbook not found at:\n",
    gbd_rr_path,
    "\nEnsure it is available in data-raw/GBD_RR_2019/.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

gbd_rr_matrix <- read_gbd_bmi_rr(path = gbd_rr_path)

rr_obesity_gbd <- transform_bmi_relative_risks(
  rr_matrix = gbd_rr_matrix,
bmi_reference = 22,
bmi_overweight = 27.5,
bmi_obesity = 32.5
)
```

### 5.4 Cost Data Loading and Validation

Published costs are expressed in thousands of 2018 euros and reflect the Portuguese National Health Service perspective reported by Borges et al. [@Borges2025].

Published INSEF 2015 prevalence estimates are retained as comparator and audit inputs. PAFs are calculated using simulated 2018 age-sex-specific prevalence of overweight and obesity.

```{r}
#| label: load-cost-inputs
#| include: false

costs_2018 <- obesity_direct_costs_2018()
pafs_ow_ob <- obesity_overweight_pafs()
cost_mapping <- obesity_cost_outcome_mapping()
published_prevalence_2018 <- obesity_prevalence_2018()

required_cost_columns <- c(
  "disease_group",
  "inpatient",
  "outpatient",
  "pharmacological",
  "total"
)

missing_cost_columns <- setdiff(
  required_cost_columns,
  names(costs_2018)
)

if (length(missing_cost_columns) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "`obesity_direct_costs_2018()` lacks required columns: ",
    paste(missing_cost_columns, collapse = ", "),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}
```


### 5.5 High-BMI Attributable Cost Scenario for 2018

Age- and sex-specific PAFs are calculated from simulated 2018 prevalence of overweight and obesity and then applied to the published 2018 disease-group cost matrix.

Published direct treatment costs for overweight and obesity are included separately at 100% attribution. Depression is excluded from the attributable total because no BMI-to-depression relative-risk function is applied.

```{r}
#| label: run-module3-costs
#| cache: false

exclude_groups <- c("obesity_overweight", "depression")

direct_obesity_costs <- costs_2018 |>
  filter(disease_group == "obesity_overweight")

depression_costs <- costs_2018 |>
  filter(disease_group == "depression")

costs_gbd <- costs_2018 |>
  filter(!disease_group %in% exclude_groups)

if (nrow(direct_obesity_costs) != 1L) {
  stop("Expected exactly one `obesity_overweight` cost row.", call. = FALSE)
}
if (nrow(depression_costs) != 1L) {
  stop("Expected exactly one `depression` cost row.", call. = FALSE)
}

# ── Step 1: age- and sex-specific simulated prevalence at 2018 ─────────────
# extract_simulated_obesity_prevalence_by_age_sex() now returns both
# p_overweight and p_obesity so the two-category PAF formula can be applied.
prevalence_age_sex_2018 <- extract_simulated_obesity_prevalence_by_age_sex(
  simulation_output = simulation_historical,
  year              = 2018L,
  weight_col        = "survey_weight"
)

# Also keep sex-level totals for trajectory scaling and the prevalence table
prevalence_2018_sim <- simulation_historical |>
  filter(alive, year == 2018L) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(
    p_overweight = weighted.mean(bmi >= 25 & bmi < 30, w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    p_obesity    = weighted.mean(bmi >= 30,             w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    p_high_bmi   = weighted.mean(bmi >= 25,             w = survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(sex = dplyr::recode(sex, men = "Males", women = "Females"))

# ── Step 2: age- and sex-specific two-category PAFs ────────────────────────
# Two exposure categories, each evaluated at a representative BMI:
#   Overweight: representative BMI 27.5 kg/m² vs reference 22 kg/m²
#   Obesity:    representative BMI 32.5 kg/m² vs reference 22 kg/m²
# Multi-category formula: PAF = [p_OW*(RR_OW-1) + p_OB*(RR_OB-1)] /
#                               [1 + p_OW*(RR_OW-1) + p_OB*(RR_OB-1)]
pafs_high_bmi <- calculate_obesity_pafs_age_sex(
  rr_matrix          = gbd_rr_matrix,
  prevalence_age_sex = prevalence_age_sex_2018,
  bmi_reference      = 22,
  bmi_overweight     = 27.5,
  bmi_obesity        = 32.5
)

# ── Step 3: apply PAFs to published 2018 disease costs ─────────────────────
obesity_costs <- calculate_obesity_costs_age_sex(
  paf_by_outcome  = pafs_high_bmi$paf_by_outcome,
  outcome_mapping = cost_mapping,
  costs_dro       = costs_gbd
)

required_cost_outputs <- c("costs_by_group", "paf_by_group", "total_costs")
missing_cost_outputs  <- setdiff(required_cost_outputs, names(obesity_costs))
if (length(missing_cost_outputs) > 0L) {
  stop(
    "`calculate_obesity_costs_age_sex()` is missing output(s): ",
    paste(missing_cost_outputs, collapse = ", "),
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

write_result_csv(prevalence_2018_sim,            "module3_simulated_bmi_prevalence_2018.csv")
write_result_csv(pafs_high_bmi$paf_by_outcome,   "module3_high_bmi_pafs_by_outcome_2018.csv")
write_result_csv(obesity_costs$costs_by_group,   "module3_high_bmi_costs_by_group_2018.csv")
```

```{r}

#| label: create-module3-combined-total
#| include: false

required_gbd_total_columns <- c(
  "inpatient_obesity_total",
  "outpatient_obesity_total",
  "pharmacological_obesity_total",
  "total_obesity"
)

missing_gbd_total_columns <- setdiff(

if (length(missing_gbd_total_columns) > 0L) {

required_published_cost_columns <- c(

if (length(missing_published_cost_columns) > 0L) {

  )
}

gbd_cost_total <- obesity_costs$total_costs |>
  summarise(
    inpatient_k_eur = sum(inpatient_obesity_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    outpatient_k_eur = sum(outpatient_obesity_total, na.rm = TRUE),
    pharmacological_k_eur = sum(
      pharmacological_obesity_total,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    total_k_eur = sum(total_obesity, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

direct_obesity_total <- direct_obesity_costs |>
  summarise(
    inpatient_k_eur = sum(inpatient, na.rm = TRUE),
    outpatient_k_eur = sum(outpatient, na.rm = TRUE),
    pharmacological_k_eur = sum(pharmacological, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_k_eur = sum(total, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

cost_components <- bind_rows(
  gbd_cost_total |>
    mutate(component = "GBD-based high-BMI-attributable downstream costs"),
  direct_obesity_total |>
    mutate(component = "Direct overweight-and-obesity treatment costs")
)



combined_obesity_cost_total <- bind_rows(
  cost_components,
  cost_components |>
    summarise(
      component = "Combined high-BMI-attributable costs",
      inpatient_k_eur = sum(inpatient_k_eur, na.rm = TRUE),
      outpatient_k_eur = sum(outpatient_k_eur, na.rm = TRUE),
      pharmacological_k_eur = sum(pharmacological_k_eur, na.rm = TRUE),
      total_k_eur = sum(total_k_eur, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
) |>
  select(
    component,
    inpatient_k_eur,
    outpatient_k_eur,
    pharmacological_k_eur,
    total_k_eur
  )

write_result_csv(
  combined_obesity_cost_total,
  "module3_combined_obesity_cost_total_2018.csv"
)
```

### 5.6 Interpretation and Limitations

This is an exploratory, top-down, prevalence-based high-BMI attributable-cost scenario. The 2018 estimate is not intended to reproduce the Borges et al. total because it uses simulated rather than INSEF-based exposure prevalence and a two-category representative-BMI approximation to the continuous GBD exposure distribution.

Published disease-group costs are held at 2018 levels. The analysis does not model changes in healthcare use, treatment mix, prices, disease incidence, survival, comorbidity, or cost per case.

The scenario has not been independently validated against another Portuguese cost year, administrative-cost source, or patient-level healthcare-use dataset.

### 5.7 Prevalence-Scaled High-BMI Cost Trajectories, 2018–2040

Annual high-BMI-attributable cost scenarios are projected by scaling the combined 2018 cost estimate in proportion to simulated high-BMI prevalence, defined as BMI ≥25 kg/m²:

\[
C_t =
C_{2018}
\times
\frac{p_{\mathrm{highBMI},t}}
     {p_{\mathrm{highBMI},2018}},
\]

where \(C_{2018}\) is the combined 2018 high-BMI-attributable cost scenario and \(p_{\mathrm{highBMI},t}\) is simulated high-BMI prevalence in year \(t\).

This prevalence-scaling approach holds the 2018 disease-cost structure, age-sex composition, category-specific relative risks, and the relative distribution of overweight and obesity constant. It does not recalculate disease-specific age-sex PAFs for subsequent years and should not be interpreted as an independently validated forecast of Portuguese healthcare expenditure.

Annual resource costs are reported in constant 2018 euros and inflation-adjusted 2026 euros. For economic-evaluation presentation, costs after 2026 are also discounted to 2026 present value at an annual rate of 3%. Discounted values are presented separately and do not represent annual healthcare-resource burden.

```{r}
#| label: cost-trajectory-inputs
#| include: false

cpi_2026 <- 117.22
discount_rate <- 0.03

sim_prev_combined <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(alive, year >= 2018L, year <= 2040L) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    high_bmi_prev = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 25,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

sim_prev_detail <- simulation_historical |>
  dplyr::filter(alive, year >= 2018L, year <= 2040L) |>
  dplyr::group_by(year, sex, education_level) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    high_bmi_prev = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 25,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    overweight_prev = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 25 & bmi < 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    obesity_prev = weighted.mean(
      bmi >= 30,
      w = survey_weight,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    population_weight = sum(survey_weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

base_total_cost_2018 <- combined_obesity_cost_total |>
  dplyr::filter(component == "Combined high-BMI-attributable costs") |>
  dplyr::pull(total_k_eur)

if (length(base_total_cost_2018) != 1L || is.na(base_total_cost_2018)) {
  stop(
    "Expected exactly one combined 2018 high-BMI baseline cost.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}

high_bmi_prev_2018 <- sim_prev_combined |>
  dplyr::filter(year == 2018L) |>
  dplyr::pull(high_bmi_prev)

if (length(high_bmi_prev_2018) != 1L ||
    is.na(high_bmi_prev_2018) ||
    high_bmi_prev_2018 <= 0) {
  stop(
    "Simulated 2018 high-BMI prevalence must be one positive value.",
    call. = FALSE
  )
}
```

```{r}
#| label: run-cost-trajectory
#| cache: false

cost_trajectory <- sim_prev_combined |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    prevalence_scale = high_bmi_prev / high_bmi_prev_2018,
    cost_constant_2018eur = base_total_cost_2018 * prevalence_scale,
    cost_2026eur_undiscounted = cost_constant_2018eur * (cpi_2026 / 100),
    discount_factor = dplyr::if_else(
      year > 2026L,
      1 / ((1 + discount_rate) ^ (year - 2026L)),
      1
    ),
    cost_2026pv = cost_2026eur_undiscounted * discount_factor
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    high_bmi_prev,
    prevalence_scale,
    discount_factor,
    cost_constant_2018eur,
    cost_2026eur_undiscounted,
    cost_2026pv
  )

write_result_csv(
  cost_trajectory,
  "module3_high_bmi_cost_trajectory_2018_2040.csv"
)

write_result_csv(
  sim_prev_detail,
  "module3_high_bmi_prevalence_by_sex_education.csv"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cost-trajectory
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Prevalence-scaled exploratory high-BMI-attributable direct medical cost scenarios, 2018–2040. Costs are scaled from the combined 2018 high-BMI cost scenario in proportion to simulated high-BMI prevalence (BMI ≥25 kg/m²) and are expressed in constant 2018 euros and inflation-adjusted 2026 euros. Both series represent undiscounted annual resource-cost scenarios, not externally validated forecasts of healthcare expenditure."

cost_trajectory |>
  dplyr::select(
    year,
    cost_constant_2018eur,
    cost_2026eur_undiscounted
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      cost_constant_2018eur,
      cost_2026eur_undiscounted
    ),
    names_to = "series",
    values_to = "cost_k_eur"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    series = dplyr::recode(
      series,
      cost_constant_2018eur = "Annual resource cost (constant 2018€)",
      cost_2026eur_undiscounted = "Annual resource cost (2026€)"

  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Annual cost (k€)",
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Package Availability and Release Status

PONTE-PT remains under active development. This report used the development state of the version-controlled source repository.

Before a formal release, project documentation will specify the package version and Git commit identifier; R version and operating system; package dependencies and versions; input-data sources, cleaning procedures, and linkage decisions; simulation settings; and automated test results.

Following development and review, the PONTE-PT source code is intended to be made publicly available through GitHub under an appropriate open-source licence. The version used for any published analysis will be archived in a persistent repository and assigned a citable identifier.

* * *

## Priorities for Co-author Review

At this stage, the principal review questions concern the scientific defensibility of the model structure and annual event sequence; the adequacy and priority improvements of the synthetic-cohort BMI-transition approach; and the validation and uncertainty analyses required before results can inform policy. Comments on presentation and formatting are welcome but secondary.

1. Is the conceptual model structure and annual event sequence appropriate for the intended policy applications?
2. Are the Portuguese inputs and their intended replacements for other jurisdictions correctly identified in the transferability table?
3. Is the synthetic-cohort annual BMI-transition approach, including binary education grouping and quadratic age extrapolation beyond age 79, acceptable given the available data?
4. Are the current validation labels and limitations sufficiently transparent?
